## Example 1.5 {#dc1-example-1-5 .dc-lesson}

<p>Let <span data-math="y=e^{f(x)}"></span>. Let <span data-math="u=f(x)"></span>. Use the chain rule <span data-math="\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\times\frac{du}{dx}"></span> to prove that <span data-math="\frac{dy}{dx}=f'(x)e^{f(x)}"></span>.</p>
<div class="takeaway">The exponent can now be any differentiable function.</div>
<div class="dc-working fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><div aria-live="polite"><div class="dc-step"><span data-math="\frac{dy}{du}=e^u,\qquad\frac{du}{dx}={\color{#b55224}f\prime(x)}"></span></div><div class="dc-step"><span data-math="\frac{dy}{dx}=e^u{\color{#b55224}f\prime(x)}={\color{#b55224}f\prime(x)}e^{f(x)}"></span></div></div></div><p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 4 · Example 1.5</p>

::: notes
The statement to prove is part of the original question and remains visible. Complete the short proof in OneNote, then press Next once to reveal both lines together to consolidate. Previous hides the whole proof. The entire exponent remains inside the exponential. Differentiate it separately and multiply. Follow-up for the next slide: “If the base were a rather than e, which extra constant would appear?” ln a. About three minutes.
